question: What is the main goal of medical treatment for someone with hyperthyroidism?

options.A: Replacing deficient thyroid hormones with synthetic T4
options.B: Blocking all adrenaline receptors in the central nervous system
options.C: Permanently destroying the thyroid gland using chemical agents
options.D: Restoring a normal metabolic state known as euthyroidism

explanation: We want to bring those high hormone levels back down to a healthy, balanced state called euthyroidism. You've got this! [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h1)

question: Why don't patients feel immediate symptom relief right after starting antithyroid medication?

options.A: Body tissues require time to build resistance against excess circulating hormones
options.B: The liver takes at least two weeks to activate the chemical structure of the drug
options.C: The thyroid gland stores large amounts of preformed hormone that must be used up first
options.D: Digestive enzymes in the stomach destroy the medication during the first fortnight

explanation: Think of the thyroid like a full warehouse. It has to clear out its stored hormones before the patient starts feeling better! [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h1)

question: Which enzyme do thioamide medications block to stop the thyroid from making too many hormones?
explanation: Thioamides target thyroid peroxidase, which is the key enzyme the gland needs to build new hormones. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h2)

question: What extra job does propylthiouracil (PTU) do that methimazole doesn't?

options.A: Stimulating the pituitary gland to stop releasing TSH
options.B: Binding directly to circulating T3 molecules in the blood
options.C: Destroying existing thyroid tissue through direct radiation
options.D: Inhibiting the peripheral conversion of T4 into T3

explanation: Besides stopping new hormone production, PTU also slows down how T4 turns into the active T3 hormone in the body's tissues. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h2)

question: Why is propylthiouracil (PTU) preferred over methimazole during early pregnancy?

options.A: Methimazole is linked to specific birth defects during early pregnancy
options.B: PTU crosses the human placenta much faster than methimazole
options.C: PTU stays active in pregnant women for up to one full week
options.D: Methimazole stimulates uterine contractions and causes early labor

explanation: We avoid methimazole in the first trimester because it carries a risk of birth defects, making PTU the safer choice for mum and baby. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h3)

question: A pregnant patient in her 8th week comes in with severe hyperthyroidism. Which medication should the nurse expect the doctor to order?
explanation: Spot on! PTU is the go-to medication during the first trimester of pregnancy to keep the baby safe from methimazole's risks. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h3)

question: Which condition is a strict, absolute 'no-go' for giving radioactive iodine (I-131) therapy?
explanation: Radioactive iodine can cross the placenta and harm the baby's developing thyroid, so pregnancy is an absolute contraindication. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h4)

question: What is the most common long-term result for patients who receive radioactive iodine treatment?

options.A: The need for lifelong maintenance doses of propylthiouracil
options.B: Spontaneous recovery of normal thyroid function within five years
options.C: Complete physical removal of the thyroid gland through scarring
options.D: Permanent hypothyroidism requiring lifelong hormone replacement

explanation: Because the radiation quiets down the gland so well, many patients end up with an underactive thyroid and take daily thyroxine tablets. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h4)

question: What is the main reason a nurse gives a beta-blocker to someone with hyperthyroidism?

options.A: Controlling rapid heart rate, tremors, and anxiety symptoms
options.B: Replacing depleted stores of thyroxine in peripheral tissues
options.C: Permanently destroying hyperactive thyroid cells with radiation
options.D: Stopping the thyroid gland from synthesizing new hormones

explanation: Beta-blockers act like a calming shield, quickly easing that racing heart, shaking, and jittery feeling while other meds kick in. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h5)

question: What is the most crucial check a nurse must perform before giving a scheduled dose of propranolol?
explanation: Always check that pulse! Beta-blockers lower the heart rate, so we need to make sure it isn't already too slow before giving the drug. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h5)

question: Why do doctors prescribe strong iodine solutions like Lugol's solution right before a thyroid surgery?

options.A: To prevent allergic reactions to general anesthesia agents
options.B: To permanently destroy overactive hormone-producing cells
options.C: To reduce the size and blood supply of the thyroid gland
options.D: To block peripheral conversion of T4 into active T3

explanation: Giving iodine beforehand shrinks the thyroid and makes it less bloody, which helps prevent heavy bleeding during the operation. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h6)

question: Why can't high-dose iodine solutions be used as a long-term treatment for hyperthyroidism?

options.A: The liver breaks down the iodine molecules before they reach the neck
options.B: Patients rapidly develop severe lifelong addiction to the taste of iodine
options.C: The thyroid gland escapes from the blocking effect after 10 to 14 days
options.D: Prolonged use permanently stains the teeth and oral mucous membranes

explanation: The thyroid is clever—it adjusts to the high iodine levels quickly, meaning the blocking effect wears off in about two weeks. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h6)

question: If a patient taking a thioamide medication reports which symptom, should you suspect a serious blood issue like agranulocytosis?
explanation: Always take a new fever and sore throat seriously with these meds; it can be an early warning sign of a dangerously low white blood cell count. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h7)

question: What is the major black-box warning linked to the long-term use of propylthiouracil (PTU)?

options.A: Severe liver injury and acute liver failure
options.B: Sudden permanent blindness from optic neuritis
options.C: Massive kidney stone formation and renal colic
options.D: Rapid deterioration of bone density and fractures

explanation: PTU carries a serious warning about liver damage, which is why nurses always keep an eye out for liver function test results. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h7)

question: Why do many hyperthyroid patients in low-resource settings often arrive at the hospital with very advanced illness?

options.A: Delays in reaching specialized care and initial use of traditional remedies
options.B: Widespread mandatory fortification of local staple foods with thyroxine
options.C: Genetic mutations that make local strains of the disease grow faster
options.D: Strict government bans on importing standard antithyroid medicines

explanation: Long distances to health facilities and trying local herbal remedies first often mean patients only reach the hospital when their illness is quite advanced. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h8)

question: A nurse is teaching an outpatient about methimazole. Which instruction is the most important to emphasize before they leave?

options.A: Stop taking the medication as soon as your hand tremors stop
options.B: Avoid eating all green leafy vegetables while on this therapy
options.C: Report any yellowing of the eyes or dark urine immediately
options.D: Double your next dose if you happen to forget taking yesterday's pill

explanation: Spotting liver trouble early is life-saving! Yellow eyes (jaundice) or dark urine mean they need to call the clinic right away. [learn more](GNS223_U7_T3#GNS223_U7_T3_h8)
